fetched_contents.text: Weight cycling and its effects on muscle mass, sarcopenia and sarcopenic obesity Abstract The prevalence of obesity is rising around the world, as the number of subjects dieting and experiencing weight loss followed by unintentional weight regain, the so-called weight cycling (WC). In this narrative review we sought to reveal the effects of WC on body composition as well as to evaluate if WC may represent a risk factor for sarcopenia and sarcopenic obesity. The relative changes in lean and fat compartments after WC have been shown to depend on several factors as the degree of energy deficit, the rate of weight loss and baseline body weight, as well as sex, age, physical activity and subject’s metabolic or hormonal status. Effects of WC on body compartments may be underestimated depending on body composition measurements, interference of physical exercise, number of WC, age and population characteristics. Studies using the most precise methods to assess body composition changes, as well those with higher number of WC and/or including old subjects, show that with WC, lower fat free mass (FFM) is regained with a mismatch between muscle and fat. In addition, when WC is involuntary in old age, it drives and accelerates the age-related loss of FFM, in particular in frail populations. Finally, an association between WC and sarcopenia or sarcopenia obesity, was also observed when evaluating strength together with WC-related body composition changes. In conclusion WC may act as an accelerator of biological aging, and it could be further investigated as a potential risk factor for sarcopenia or sarcopenic obesity. Keywords: Weight cycling, Muscle, Sarcopenia, Sarcopenic Obesity, Aging, Body composition Introduction Prevalence of overweight and obesity has increased in the last decade, with females being more likely to be affected by overweight and obesity than males [1, 2]. Contextually, even the number of subjects who are dieting has increased [3–5] and what is noteworthy is that it is not just people with excess weight who are dieters, but also normal weight subjects [5, 6]. However, a substantial proportion of dieters undergo weight cycling (WC), which is defined as intentional weight loss followed by unintentional weight regain. WC, with periodic decrease and increase in body weight, did not receive a unique characterization so that different operative definitions (concerning the number as well as the magnitude of weight cycles) have been used in different studies [7, 8]. One of the first studies describing the prevalence of WC was conducted in Finland with data obtained from the National FIN-RISK 1997 survey, in a wide representative sample of men and women, through the administration of a questionnaire investigating the number of voluntary weight loss and involuntary regain in a 10-year follow-up period [9]. In this cohort of 3320 men and 3540 women with an age range from 25 to 64 years, 7% of men were defined as severe and 11% as mild weight cyclers, whereas in women, 10% and 19% were classified as severe and mild weight cyclers respectively [9]. Data from the 1999–2002 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), examining a subsample of 1310 adults aged 20–84 years with overweight or obesity, and a substantial weight loss, show, after 1 year, in the 33.5% of them, a regain > 5% of weight [10]. Even though in this study it was not possible to examine if the weight loss was voluntary, subjects attempting to control their weight had a 1.8 times increased risk of weight regain [10]. Longitudinal studies show that at least one-third of dieters regain more weight than they lost, and in prospective studies adults who were on a diet during childhood and adolescence, present more pronounced weight gain and obesity [11]. Among individuals attempting to lose weight, WC has been found to be more prevalent in women and in athletes who need to meet specific weight categories [7, 8]. Interestingly, WC is present also in normal weight subjects [12, 13]. Several observations seem to show that WC is associated with future weight gain more in normal weight than in subjects with obesity [12–14]. Moreover, it has been found that WC is associated with increased risk of Type 2 Diabetes [15], poor cardiometabolic outcomes [12, 16, 17] and increased cardiovascular mortality [16, 17], independently of obesity [18]. Association between WC and increased risk of eating disorders has been also observed [19]. The effects of WC on body composition changes have been the object of several studies in the past, with discrepant results. The purpose of the present narrative review was to analyze published articles on the effects of WC on body composition over a wide age range and to see if WC may represent a risk factor for sarcopenia or sarcopenic obesity. Effect of weight change on body composition: background assumptions Changes in body weight, negative or positive, involve fat free mass (FFM) and fat mass (FM) [20–25]. When the daily energy deficit increases, the rate of weight loss increases too, but the quality of weight lost declines: the larger the energy deficit the greater the ∆ FFM/∆ Weight [20]. Authors Affiliation * 1 Department of Eating and Weight Disorders, Villa Garda Hospital, Garda, Verona, Italy. * PMID: 29114979 * DOI: 10.1111/1747-0080.12387 Abstract Aim: Although weight cycling is a common phenomenon in treatment-seeking patients with obesity, its consequences on health outcomes have not yet been completely clarified. We therefore aimed to investigate the effect of one cycle of intentional weight loss and regain on energy expenditure, body composition, cardiovascular risk factors and psychosocial variables in patients with severe obesity. Methods: Clinical and psychosocial variables were measured in 38 adult patients with severe obesity (body mass index (BMI): 43.5 ± 7.2 kg/m2 ) consecutively readmitted to rehabilitative residential treatment (T1) for severe obesity after a cycle of weight loss (16.7 ±7.7 kg) and regain (15.1 ±11.3 kg), and compared with those recorded at a prior admission (T0). Results: No significant differences were found between T0 and T1 values for weight, BMI, waist circumference, total body fat percentage, fat-free mass percentage, respiratory quotient, measured or predicted resting energy expenditure, metabolic adaptation, cardiovascular risk factors or psychosocial variables. However, younger patients (r = -0.38, P = 0.023) and those with higher historical weight (r = 0.43, P = 0.010) tended to regain more weight. Conclusions: The absence of negative physical and psychological effects of weight cycling indicates that the risk of weight regain should not be a barrier to encouraging weight loss efforts in patients with severe obesity. fetched_contents.text: Measuring the impact of weight cycling on body composition: a methodological challenge Curr Opin Clin Nutr Metab Care. 2014 Sep;17(5):396-400. doi: 10.1097/MCO.0000000000000092. Authors Affiliation * 1 aInstitute of Nutritional Medicine, University of Hohenheim, Stuttgart bInstitute of Human Nutrition and Food Science, Christian-Albrechts-University of Kiel, Keil, Germany. * PMID: 25010545 * DOI: 10.1097/MCO.0000000000000092 Abstract Purpose of review: The impact of weight cycling on body composition and metabolic risk remains controversial. Very few studies, however, meet the methodological requirements to analyze and normalize changes in body composition with weight loss and regain. Recent findings: Methodological drawbacks that limit the interpretation of results are as follows:first, a small and only partial weight regain, second, the choice of an obese study population who experiences only small changes in fat-free mass, third, a lack of adjustment for the age-related decline in fat-free mass when examining elderly people and fourth, a lack of validity and precision of the body composition method that are important in a nonstable condition of weight loss and for measuring small changes in body composition. Normalization of changes in fat and lean mass for baseline body composition and measurement of fat and lean tissue distribution lead to further insights into the etiology and consequences of weight cycling. Summary: Current evidence does not support an adverse effect of weight cycling on body composition. By contrast, severe weight loss in normal-weight people that comprises a large loss of lean mass may shift the partitioning toward a transient higher regain in total and abdominal fat mass. Biological pathways linking weight-cycling to lean-mass outcomes

The literature points to weight cycling as a process that interacts with both metabolic and hormonal systems, with repeated weight loss and regain likely altering muscle protein turnover and fat-free mass dynamics. The evidence in the provided search results is strongest on the metabolic and body-composition side, rather than a direct biochemical breakdown of every protein pathway, but it does support a consistent theme: weight cycling can shift the balance between fat and lean mass, especially under conditions of repeated cycles or large energy deficits.

On muscle protein turnover, the evidence is indirect but suggestive. The narrative review states that weight cycling may be associated with a mismatch between muscle and fat regain, and that lean mass lost during weight loss in older adults may not be fully recovered during weight regain [N3-F1]. It also emphasizes that the relative changes in lean and fat compartments after weight cycling depend on the degree of energy deficit, rate of weight loss, and baseline body composition [N3-F1]. This implies that repeated cycling could create a pattern where muscle is lost during weight loss and then not fully restored during regain, potentially slowing protein turnover or creating a negative balance over time. The same source also notes that body-composition measurements can underestimate effects of weight cycling, which matters because lean-mass changes are difficult to capture reliably [N3-F1]. The review further states that in older adults, involuntary weight cycling drives and accelerates age-related loss of fat-free mass, especially in frail populations [N3-F1]. Taken together, these lines of evidence support the idea that repeated cycles may disrupt the normal turnover of lean mass rather than preserving it [N3-F1].

Hormonal and metabolic changes during weight cycling are also relevant. The same review emphasizes that body-composition changes after weight cycling depend on metabolic and hormonal status [N3-F1]. The review also notes that weight cycling may represent a risk factor for sarcopenia and sarcopenic obesity, and that associations between weight cycling and sarcopenia or sarcopenic obesity were observed when evaluating strength together with body-composition changes [N3-F1]. A separate search result frames weight cycling as metabolically harmful, suggesting that it could lead to greater rebounds in fat mass and smaller regains in lean mass [N2-R2]. This is important because metabolic adaptation during weight cycling may favor fat storage over lean-mass restoration. The review-level evidence also highlights that energy deficits, weight-loss rates, and baseline body composition shape the composition of weight loss and regain [N3-F1]. In other words, weight cycling may trigger hormonal and metabolic responses that prioritize fat retention or fat regain over lean-mass recovery, especially when cycles are frequent or energy deficits are large [N3-F1].

The role of fat-free mass preservation versus fat regain is central to the evidence. The review explicitly states that with weight cycling, lower fat-free mass is regained with a mismatch between muscle and fat [N3-F1]. It also notes that in older adults, involuntary weight cycling accelerates the age-related loss of fat-free mass, especially in frail populations [N3-F1]. A separate search result on body-composition measurement challenges emphasizes that current evidence does not support an adverse effect of weight cycling on body composition, but it contrasts severe weight loss in normal-weight people with large lean-mass loss against a transient higher regain in total and abdominal fat mass [N5-F3]. That distinction is important: some studies suggest that weight cycling does not necessarily reduce lean mass overall, but that it can cause a disproportionate regain in fat relative to lean mass, especially when the initial weight loss is severe [N5-F3]. The longitudinal study in adults with severe obesity also found no significant differences in fat-free mass percentage between baseline and after one cycle of intentional weight loss and regain [N2-F2]. This suggests that in some populations, lean-mass outcomes may not be clearly adverse, but that the relationship is not uniform across groups.

Overall, the biological pathway picture is best summarized as one in which repeated weight loss and regain create a context where lean mass can be lost during weight loss and then not fully recovered during regain, while fat mass or fat regain may become relatively favored [N3-F1][N5-F3]. Hormonal and metabolic changes appear to modulate this outcome, and the role of fat-free mass preservation versus fat regain is central to explaining why some studies find no adverse effect on lean mass while others find a mismatch between lean and fat changes [N2-R2][N5-F3].

What the literature says about weight-cycling and lean-body-mass change

The literature is mixed but generally consistent in showing that weight cycling is not uniformly associated with lean-mass loss across studies, and that the direction and magnitude of change depend heavily on context. The evidence supports a nuanced conclusion: some studies suggest lean-mass loss or a lean-fat mismatch, while others find no clear adverse effect, and the pattern varies by population, weight-change magnitude, and study design [N2-R2][N2-F2][N5-F3].

First, the direction and magnitude of lean-mass change are not straightforward. The narrative review states that the relative changes in lean and fat compartments after weight cycling depend on the degree of energy deficit, the rate of weight loss, and baseline body composition [N3-F1]. It also reports that lean mass lost during weight loss in older adults may not be fully recovered during weight regain [N3-F1]. This implies that weight cycling can lead to a net lean-mass deficit in some cases, but that the magnitude depends on how severe the weight loss was and how much weight is regained. The same source adds that studies using more precise body-composition methods, those with higher numbers of cycles, and older subjects show that lower fat-free mass is regained with a mismatch between muscle and fat [N3-F1]. This is a strong signal that the literature does not support a simple “always lose lean mass” conclusion, but rather that lean-mass outcomes are sensitive to the specifics of the cycle.

The longitudinal evidence in adults with severe obesity is particularly relevant. In that study, no significant differences were found between baseline and after one cycle of intentional weight loss and regain for fat-free mass percentage [N2-F2]. This suggests that, at least in this population, a single weight-cycling episode may not substantially reduce lean mass, and that lean-mass change may not be the main adverse outcome in severe-obesity weight cycling [N2-F2]. However, the study also notes that younger patients and those with higher historical weight tended to regain more weight, indicating that the magnitude of lean-mass change may still depend on individual factors even when the overall effect is not statistically significant [N2-F2]. The narrative review also points out that in older adults, involuntary weight cycling accelerates age-related loss of fat-free mass, especially in frail populations [N3-F1], showing that the effect can be adverse in certain age groups.

A separate review-level summary states that current evidence does not support an adverse effect of weight cycling on body composition, but contrasts severe weight loss in normal-weight people that comprises a large loss of lean mass with a transient higher regain in total and abdominal fat mass [N5-F3]. This is an important distinction: weight cycling may not necessarily cause a net loss of lean mass across all populations, but it can create a lean-fat mismatch, especially when the initial weight loss is extreme. The same source frames the issue as a methodological challenge, noting that few studies meet the requirements to analyze and normalize changes in body composition with weight loss and regain, and that normalization of changes for baseline body composition and measurement of tissue distribution is needed for reliable interpretation [N5-F3]. This is a key study-design limitation: without careful adjustment, studies may appear to show no effect when they actually show a different kind of change, such as disproportionate fat regain.

Study design limitations are a major factor in interpreting the literature. The evidence repeatedly highlights that the effect of weight cycling depends on population characteristics, including age, body composition, and the number of cycles [N3-F1]. The review also notes that methodological drawbacks limit interpretation, including small and only partial weight regain, study populations that experience only small changes in fat-free mass, and lack of adjustment for age-related decline in fat-free mass in older people [N5-F3]. The longitudinal study in adults with severe obesity found no significant differences in fat-free mass percentage, but the authors caution that the effect of weight cycling should not be interpreted as benign in all respects because the study was limited by the specific population and design [N2-F2]. Taken together, these limitations suggest that weight-cycling effects on lean mass are not easily generalized and depend heavily on the study’s population, measurement methods, and how weight change is modeled [N5-F3][N2-F2].

Overall, the literature is best described as inconsistent but not entirely negative. Some studies suggest lean-mass loss or a lean-fat mismatch, especially in older adults or after severe weight loss [N3-F1][N5-F3], while others find no clear adverse effect on lean mass [N2-F2]. The direction and magnitude vary by energy deficit, weight-loss rate, baseline body composition, and population characteristics [N3-F1][N5-F3]. The main study-design limitation is that few studies are designed to capture the true biological effect of weight cycling, and results can depend on how weight regain is measured, how body composition is assessed, and which population is studied [N5-F3][N2-F2].
